Overuse injuries occur if repetitive submaximal stress is applied to a muscle, tendon, or
bone, ultimately resulting in microtrauma if adequate time to heal or repair has not been
allotted.1-3
Occur in absence of a single, identifiable traumatic cause
Include apophyseal injuries and physeal stress injuries in youth athletes
Sport specialization is associated with increased risk of overuse injuries.

Overview
Overuse is one of the most common etiologic factors contributing to injury in pediatric
and adolescent athletes. Year-round training, sport specialization, and participation with
multiple teams have replaced recreational activities, which traditionally provided young
athletes the opportunity to develop a wide range of skills. As youth sports participation
has become more specialized, the incidence of overuse injuries in children and
adolescent athletes has been increasing.
Epidemiology
Lower extremity overuse injuries are most common.
Overuse injury rates are higher in female athletes compared with male athletes in sex-
comparable sports.4

Epidemiology
Approximately 30 to 45 million individuals aged 6 to 18 years participate in organized
sports. Overuse injuries constitute almost 50% of injuries presenting to pediatric sports
medicine practices5 (Table 1). Approximately 50% of overuse injuries in high school
athletes result in more than 1 week of loss from sports participation.6 Overuse injuries
tend to be underestimated in the scientific literature because most epidemiologic
studies define injury as requiring time loss from participation.2

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Pediatric/adolescent athletes
Overuse physeal injuries may involve tendinous attachments (traction apophysitis—Osgood-
Schlatter disease, Sinding-Larsen-Johansson syndrome [Figure 1], Sever disease) and
overloading of the long bone physis (Little Leaguer’s shoulder [Figure 2], distal radial physeal
injury in gymnasts).
Rapid growth spurts result in rapid long bone growth, leaving inadequate time for
compensatory elongation and flexibility of the accompanying muscle-tendon units.
Strength imbalances on opposite sides of a joint may result from sport specialization or
poorly designed/implemented strength and conditioning programs.
Physiologic malalignment of lower extremities may predispose patients to maltracking and
stress injuries.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The hypertrophic zone, including the zone of provisional calcification, is the weakest
portion of the physis; this increases its propensity to injury during phases of rapid
growth.7 Repetitive stress on the physis may lead to widening, early calcification, and
physeal bar formation, which ultimately lead to growth disturbances, such as premature
distal radius physeal closure in gymnasts’ wrists. Growth disturbances related to physeal
stress injury also have been documented in the proximal humerus, distal femur, and
proximal tibia. A pathophysiologic theory is that repetitive stress leads to a disruption of
the metaphyseal blood supply, altered endochondral ossification of the physis, and
physeal widening caused by chondrocyte accumulation in the proliferative zone.7

Etiology
Causative factors for overuse conditions can be categorized as intrinsic or extrinsic factors.
Intrinsic factors
Anatomic (malalignment, leg-length discrepancies)
Growth and development (rapid long bone growth, associated muscle-tendon unit
inflexibility, open physes)
Nutrition (inadequate caloric intake related to excess energy expenditure, participation in
aesthetic or endurance sports, suboptimal calcium/vitamin D intake)
Preexisting conditions (chronic disease states, previous injuries, inadequately managed
fractures)
Extrinsic factors
Training errors (overtraining, insufficient rest/recovery, poor biomechanics or technique,
year-round training/competition, sport specialization)
Poor-fitting equipment (footwear, sporting equipment designed for adults used by young
athletes)
Environmental (hard playing/training surfaces)

Etiology
Intrinsic factors are unique to an individual; some are not modifiable (eg, sex, maturation
status) whereas others are potentially modifiable (eg, body mass index [BMI],
biomechanical movement patterns, anatomic alignment). Extrinsic risk factors play a role
in overuse injuries in scenarios involving rapid increase in training load over a period of
decreased activity, participation at an athletic level that exceeds an individual’s skill or
fitness level, and continuous participation at a high level of athletics or in a single activity
or sport.8
Upper Extremity Overuse Injuries in Youth Throwers
Overview

Upper extremity overuse remains prevalent in baseball and softball, with most injuries
affecting the shoulder and elbow.
Single-sport specialization at a young age, year-round participation on travel/club and/or
multiple teams, frequent training with private coaches during the off-season, and showcasing
have contributed to a disturbing injury trend in youth and high school–aged throwers.
Shoulder and elbow injuries often result from a weak link in the kinetic chain.
Poor hip flexibility, weak core strength, and poorly coordinated motions between the lower
extremities, trunk, and upper extremities result in altered mechanics of the shoulder and
elbow through the phases of throwing.

Overview
Arm pain is commonly reported among competitive baseball players. Studies on youth
pitchers aged 9 to 12 years have found that 25% to 28% and 32% to 35% of these
individuals self-report elbow or shoulder pain, respectively, at least once during a
season;9,10 70% of these instances are classified as mild pain that does not prohibit
play.11 With the paradigm shift from seasonal sport participation to year-round, high-
volume, high-intensity single-sport participation models, excessive stress applied by the
repetitive motion of an overhand throw puts young athletes at high risk for overuse
injuries.12
Epidemiology
According to The Aspen Institute’s Project Play data, baseball remains the second most
popular core sport in 2023 among children aged 6 to 12 years, behind only basketball.13
Baseball and fast-pitch softball experienced 1.2% participation increases in 2023.13
A staggering increase in ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) reconstruction has occurred in youth
and high school throwers over the past two decades; this patient population currently
accounts for approximately 40% to 50% of UCL reconstruction procedures annually.9

Epidemiology
Pitchers aged 9 to 14 years have a 5% risk of severe injury, defined as elbow/shoulder
surgery or retirement from sport because of injury, within 10 years.10 A survey of 754
youth pitchers aged 9 to 18 years revealed that a substantial portion engaged in non-
recommended activities, according to recent guidelines published by the American
Sports Medicine Institute.14 Specifically, more than 43% pitched on consecutive days,
31% pitched on multiple teams with overlapping seasons, and 19% pitched multiple
games per day, resulting in an increased risk of pitching-related arm pain. A survey by
Makhni et al15 demonstrated that 46% of youth respondents stated they were
encouraged on at least one occasion to keep playing despite arm pain. In a study of 115
high school pitchers, Erickson et al16 reported that noncompliance with Pitch Smart
guidelines is prevalent offseason and in season, with 89% of players violating at least one
component of the Pitch Smart guidelines based on a preseason survey and in-season
pitch counts.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The skeletally immature pediatric/adolescent shoulder and elbow are particularly vulnerable
to injury because of open physes.
Closure of these physes depends on sexual maturity rather than chronologic age.
Physes are relatively weak links in the kinetic chain compared with surrounding tendons,
ligaments, and bone.
Regarding the medial elbow, the immature physis represents the point of greatest weakness
until fusion of the growth plates, when the ligamentous structures are more vulnerable to
excessive valgus stress from throwing.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
As the last center to fuse, closure of the medial epicondylar apophysis defines skeletal
maturity of the elbow between ages 15 and 20 years.17 The anatomic stability of the

8/42

elbow is derived from static and dynamic components. The medial UCL, lateral collateral
ligament complex, and the ulnohumeral articulation are the primary static stabilizers,
whereas the flexor-pronator mass, which originates from the medial epicondyle, is the
primary dynamic stabilizer. The flexor-pronator mass is the initial source of resistance to
valgus stress, whereas the UCL is responsible for approximately 55% of valgus stability
during the cocking and acceleration phases of the throwing motion.18,19
The proximal humeral physis is responsible for 80% of the longitudinal growth, with
skeletal maturity usually complete by a chronologic age of 18 to 19 years in most
individuals. Humeral head retroversion commonly is observed in overhead athletes as a
beneficial adaptation to allow for greater external rotation before the anterior
ligamentous support is activated.12 The reason some throwing athletes experience
(asymptomatic) humeral head retroversion if exposed to external torque whereas other
throwing athletes experience proximal humeral epiphysiolysis, or Little Leaguer’s
shoulder remains unclear.
Etiology
Little Leaguer’s Shoulder (Proximal Humeral Epiphysiolysis)
Injury of adolescent throwers (typically aged 11 to 16 years)
Caused by shear stress from external rotation torque in the late cocking phase of throwing
Directly related to the amount and intensity of throwing; more common in pitchers, year-
round throwers
Presentation: progressively worsening shoulder pain with throwing
Physical examination: tenderness over the lateral portion of the proximal humeral physis
(shoulder in external rotation, adduction)
Imaging studies: AP, internal, and external rotation views of shoulder typically demonstrate a
spectrum of proximal humerus physeal widening, from lateral to diffuse (Figure 2).
Comparison views of the unaffected shoulder should be considered. MRIs of the shoulder
obtained in patients in whom the diagnosis is unclear based on the patient history, physical
examination, and plain radiographs often reveal proximal humeral metaphyseal bone marrow
edema, sclerosis, and posterior glenoid remodeling, reflecting physeal stress.20

Management: rest from all skilled throwing for 8 to 12 weeks; physical therapy, including a
comprehensive kinetic chain strengthening/stabilization program; followed by gradual
implementation of an interval throwing program
Little Leaguer’s Elbow (Medial Epicondylar Apophysitis/Avulsion Fracture)
General term encompassing a group of injuries
Presents in young throwers (usually aged 9 to 14 years)
Apophysitis: gradual onset, progressively worsening medial elbow pain with throwing
Avulsion fracture: acute onset, immediate medial elbow pain after a hard throw, usually
accompanied by an audible pop/crack
Many athletes typically pitch in addition to playing shortstop, third base, catcher (ie, multiple
throwing positions).
Physical examination
Apophysitis: tenderness over the medial epicondyle, pain with resisted wrist flexion
Avulsion fracture: tenderness over the medial epicondyle, limited elbow extension
Imaging studies
Apophysitis: variable widening of the medial epicondylar apophysis on AP view; radiographs
may be normal early in the disease process. Comparison views of the contralateral elbow
may be helpful.
Avulsion fracture: variable widening of the medial epicondylar apophysis with varying
fracture displacement (Figure 3); three-dimensional CT reconstruction images and axial
views may help determine anterior displacement but are associated with a risk of increased
radiation exposure.

Management
Apophysitis: restrict all skilled throwing for a minimum of 4 to 6 weeks; NSAIDs; short course
of elbow immobilization (severe cases) in combination with a thrower’s rehabilitation
program focusing on correcting kinetic chain deficits, poor biomechanics.
Avulsion fracture
Standard of care currently is controversial (nonsurgical versus surgical);21-23 debate stems
from the concern of fibrous nonunion, which frequently occurs more with nonsurgical
management.12
Minimally (<5 mm) displaced fractures: brief course of immobilization, followed by activity
restrictions and physical therapy emphasizing early range of motion
Surgical consultation advised for athletes with substantial (=5 mm) fragment displacement
and/or elbow laxity or instability.
Open reduction and internal fixation recommended for fragments with 5 mm or more of
displacement.

Return to play: accompanied by a supervised graduated throwing program; mean of 12
weeks after nonsurgical management and 7 to 8 months after surgical repair.12
UCL Overuse Injury
Sprains and partial- and full-thickness tears constitute the spectrum of UCL overuse injuries.
Tears through the anterior bundle occur more frequently than avulsion at the site of bony
attachment.
Adolescent throwers typically have more isolated damage, either partial-thickness tears or
tears at the proximal or distal attachment, compared with adult throwers who sustain more
diffuse damage throughout the length of the UCL.24
Presentation: acute (rupture) or chronic (instability, insufficiency)
Physical examination: ecchymosis, elbow effusion, loss of terminal elbow extension may be
present with acute injuries; modified milking maneuver, moving valgus stress test (70° to 120°
of elbow flexion) will elicit pain in patients with UCL insufficiency.
Imaging studies
Plain radiographs may demonstrate an avulsion fracture in patients with an acute injury. In
chronic UCL injuries, ossification of the UCL, osteophytic changes of the radiocapitellar joint
or the posteromedial compartment, loose bodies, or olecranon stress injury may be
demonstrated.25,26
Dynamic musculoskeletal ultrasonographic examination with an applied valgus stress is an
emerging imaging modality to assess UCL injuries; however, its reliability is limited, and its
quality is operator dependent.
Magnetic resonance arthrography of the elbow is the preferred imaging modality for UCL
injuries because contrast increases the sensitivity of diagnosing partial-thickness tears
compared with MRI without; however, MRI without contrast remains the preferred imaging
modality at many institutions.25,26
MRI with valgus stress is an emerging imaging modality that has potential to improve the
evaluation of the UCL in throwing athletes compared with standard MRI and conventional
patient positioning.27
Management
Nonsurgical management: indicated for low-grade partial tears confirmed via MRI/magnetic
resonance arthrography
Surgical management

UCL repair/augmentation: typically involves suture anchor repair of torn ligament and/or
high-tensile strength, nonabsorbable suture augmentation; may be indicated in young,
healthy overhead athletes with proximal or distal avulsions or partial UCL tears who are
unable to return to competition after rest/rehabilitation; often allows for a more rapid
return to play compared with UCL reconstruction.24,28
UCL reconstruction: indicated for high-grade or complete tears of the anterior bundle in
athletes desiring to return to throwing sports, throwing athletes with a partial UCL tear in
whom comprehensive rehabilitation programs have failed, and nonthrowing athletes who
remain symptomatic despite nonsurgical treatment17
Valgus Extension Overload Syndrome
Commonly presents as posteromedial elbow pain with extension during the late acceleration
and follow-through phases of throwing
Contributors to valgus extension overload syndrome include repetitive valgus stress from
throwing, adaptive elbow laxity, and UCL injury or insufficiency.21
Physical examination: reproducible pain with valgus stress testing of the elbow at 20° to 30° of
flexion while forcing the elbow into terminal extension29
Imaging studies—Radiographs may reveal osteophytes in the olecranon posteromedially or
loose bodies.
Management
Nonsurgical management: throwing restrictions, ice, NSAIDs (dexamethasone),
iontophoresis, intra-articular corticosteroids (reserved for skeletally mature throwers; used
judiciously)
Surgical management: reserved for athletes with persistent pain with loose bodies; consists
of arthroscopic débridement, loose body removal.
Olecranon Stress Injuries
Represent a spectrum of injuries ranging from olecranon stress reaction to olecranon stress
fracture (OSF)
Include proximal OSFs and avulsion fractures of the tip of the olecranon; these conditions
should be differentiated from a persistent olecranon apophysis, which is commonly identified
on radiographs of skeletally immature throwers.

Pathophysiology: rapid and repetitive valgus extension, which forces the tip of the olecranon
into the olecranon fossa; with increased UCL laxity, a compensatory increase in compression
on the medial aspect of the olecranon-olecranon fossa articulation occurs during extension.
Extensive tensile forces of the triceps on the olecranon during the acceleration of throwing
also exacerbate this process.30
Risk factors for OSF: adolescent thrower (mean age, 12 years at onset), pitcher or catcher,
playing more than 100 games/year, throwing a breaking ball, increased velocity30
Physical examination—The snapping extension test and the arm bar test often reproducibly
elicit pain in patients with OSF.30
Imaging studies—Plain radiographs (AP, lateral, and/or oblique views) should be obtained
given their cost-effectiveness and availability (Figure 4). OSFs may not appear on radiographs
if not considerable enough in size. MRI has been reported as the preferred imaging modality
for detecting OSFs by the American College of Radiology.30 MRI is associated with high
sensitivity and specificity for OSFs and can detect bony edema early and ligamentous lesions,
which is important because OSF and UCL damage often coexist.31

Management
Nonsurgical management: cessation of throwing and other valgus stress activities for 3
months, followed by rehabilitation (to address biomechanical errors, increase rotator cuff
and flexor-pronator strength); delayed radiographic union may be observed with nonsurgical
management.
Surgical management: indicated in patients in whom symptoms persist and/or athletes are
unable to return to sports activity after nonsurgical treatment; open reduction and internal
fixation (cannulated screw) is the most common surgical technique. A recent systematic
review demonstrated that 77% of patients with an elbow stress fracture opted to undergo a
surgical procedure.32 Some studies suggest that the presence of a fracture line on plain
radiographs indicates a low likelihood of spontaneous healing in overhead throwing
athletes.33
Stress Fractures
Epidemiology
Common in highly committed athletes; tend to occur in sports that involve high levels of
repetition and intensity.
Incidence of stress fractures in running/track athletes may be 10% to 20%; rate of recurrence
is approximately 10% for all athletes but as high as 50% in runners.
The tibia and metatarsals are the most common locations for lower extremity stress injuries;
however, femoral neck, proximal femur, navicular, and fibular stress injuries require clinicians
to maintain a high index of suspicion for prompt diagnosis.
Upper extremity stress fractures, although less common than lower extremity stress fractures,
occur with weight bearing and repetitive tasks (gymnasts, throwing athletes).
Pars interarticularis stress fractures are unique to adolescent athletes performing repetitive
spine extension and rotation.
Females with relative energy deficiency in sport and those with vitamin D insufficiency are at
greatest risk for stress injuries. A BMI of less than 19 kg/m2 is a risk factor for stress fracture
and extended time to return to sports activity.


Ninety-five percent of stress fractures occur in the lower extremities because of
dissipation of ground reaction forces during load-bearing tasks, such as running,
jumping, walking, or marching.34 Approximately one-half of all stress fractures occur in
the tibia.35 Stress fractures can occur in any bone that experiences abnormal stress
overload with training (eg, scaphoid in shot putters, rib in rower, lumbar vertebrae in
pitchers).
Pathophysiology
Stress fractures represent a continuous spectrum of bone injury, with stress reaction being the
initial precursor.
Accumulating microtrauma that occurs with repetitive loading ultimately results in fatigue
failure of bone that occurs in three stages: crack initiation, crack propagation, and final
fracture.
If the initial microscopic crack is not repaired and repeated loading of the bone continues, the
crack extends (crack propagation), eventually resulting in a final fracture.
In vivo, bone responds to crack initiation and propagation via a reparative biologic response
that is dependent on age, nutritional status, hormonal status, vascular supply, biomechanical
factors, and possibly genetic predisposition.
A dynamic balance exists between the accumulation of microdamage and the host repair
processes.
If microdamage accumulation exceeds the reparative response, stress fracture occurs.
Any factor that disrupts this dynamic balance may increase stress fracture risk.
Any factor that increases tensile, compressive, or torsional forces on a bone may cause an
increase in microdamage accumulation with each loading episode, especially if applied with
an abrupt increase in frequency or intensity.
Any factor that impairs the reparative biologic response, such as poor vascularity or an
altered hormonal balance, may increase the risk of a stress fracture or insufficiency fracture

Pathophysiology
A complete cycle of bone turnover and remodeling and mineralization requires 3 to 4
months. If bone cannot remodel at the pace at which loading increases, the bone

fractures.36 Wolffs law applies to bone: as stress on bone increases, the bone deforms to
accept the given force until the force exceeds the elastic range of the bone, at which time
permanent damage, such as microfracture, occurs.37
Classification
Delayed recognition or undermanagement of high-risk stress fractures tends to result in
fracture progression, nonunion, the need for surgical management, refracture, and delayed
return to sports activity.
Other fractures have a more benign natural history and are low-risk stress fractures; these
fractures tend to heal with activity modifications because of compressive forces and adequate
vascularity.
Recognizing the class of stress fracture is important for optimizing management.
Over-management of a low-risk stress fracture or undermanagement of a high-risk fracture
may result in undue loss of playing time, deconditioning, and prolonged recovery.

Classification
Stress fractures generally are classified as low-risk or high-risk depending on their
location (Table 2); those with a poor natural history are deemed high-risk and usually
require aggressive management (Table 3). MRI classification of stress fractures has been
correlated with time to return to play (Table 4). A recent generalizable clinical and
imaging classification system is associated with high intraobserver and interobserver
reliability for grading stress fractures (Table 5).

Evaluation/Diagnosis
In patients with no history of substantial repetitive loading episodes, an insufficiency fracture
or pathologic fracture must be considered, particularly in those with decreased bone density,
inadequate nutrition, or abnormal bone quality.
Radiography, bone scintigraphy, CT, and MRI are the imaging modalities used to evaluate
stress fractures. Each is associated with advantages and disadvantages, with MRI being the

9/3/26, 5:31 PM
AAOS | Overuse Conditions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000577
19/42

preferred imaging modality because of its high sensitivity and specificity.
Radiographs rarely are positive unless the injury is severe or chronic. Typically, radiographic
findings lag behind clinical symptoms for weeks to months.
Bone scintigraphy is very sensitive in identifying the presence and location of stress fractures;
however, bone scans do not reveal macroscopic fracture lines in the bone and may be positive
for as long as 2 years after the injury has clinically healed.
MRI can identify the bony edema associated with early stress concentration or reveal a
fracture line (Table 4). MRI is advantageous because it shows the surrounding soft tissues and
is most predictive of time to return to athletic activity.
Ultrasonography has been described for the imaging of stress fractures but is used much less
commonly because of its inability to penetrate the cortex. It is advantageous because no
ionizing radiation is used and a focused, real-time evaluation of the fracture can be performed.
Identifying a nonunion and assessing the amount of healing in preparation for possible
surgical management is best achieved via CT; however, this is associated with a substantial
radiation dose.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Stress fractures typically present as an insidious onset of pain but may present as an
acute onset of pain with or without prodromal pain for weeks to months. A history of
prolonged high-impact activity or a recent abrupt increase in training frequency or
intensity usually is noted. Alternatively, a recent change in the type of training (eg,
introduction of high-intensity interval training) or equipment (eg, a new brand of shoes)
may have occurred. Physical examination may reveal localized pain via direct palpation
or mechanical loading of the affected site with fulcrum testing of long bones and single-
leg hop testing. Hop testing is positive in 70% of patients with a medial tibial stress
fracture but also in one-half of patients with medial tibial stress syndrome (MTSS).38,39
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for the diagnosis of stress fracture according to
the American College of Radiology, which recommends MRI be performed if radiographs
are negative.40 MRI sensitivity is equivalent to that of bone scintigraphy (100%) but with
higher specificity (85%).37,40

Management
Management must alter the biomechanical and biologic environment to allow the reparative
processes to overcome the accumulation of microdamage at the fracture site. A holistic
approach is required to optimize healing potential.
The athlete’s biologic bone healing capacity should be evaluated. This includes review of the
athlete’s nutritional, hormonal, psychological, biomechanical, and medication status.
Relative energy deficiency in sport must be considered in any female athlete with a stress
fracture; appropriate evaluation and management should be initiated.
The fracture site also must be protected from future strain episodes via relative rest, absolute
rest, brace management, technique modifications, or surgical fixation.
Relative rest involves decreasing the frequency or magnitude of strain episodes at the stress
fracture site by modifying training volume (intensity, duration, and frequency), technique,
and equipment; by using a brace or orthosis; or by cross-training.
Absolute rest removes all strain episodes from the fracture site. This often is achieved by
having the athlete bear no weight, use crutches, and undergo immobilization.
An assessment of biomechanical risk factors, such as malalignment, should be performed to
assess the risk of stress fracture recurrence. Video running gait analysis and throwing analysis
are ideal for determining form and technique abnormalities.
The use of biophysical enhancement technologies in stress fractures, such as pulsed
ultrasonography and electrical stimulation, is not a major factor in healing an acute stress
injury.
Nutritional support with appropriate caloric intake in combination with calcium and vitamin D
supplementation is required to achieve healing and prevent recurrence. Evaluation of serum
nutritional laboratory values may be required in athletes with multiple or recurrent bony
stress injuries.
Given these principles, the management of stress fractures depends on classifying each
fracture as high or low risk.
High-risk stress fractures typically are managed via absolute rest or surgical management.
The level of risk for catastrophic injury must be seriously considered before allowing patients
with a high-risk stress fracture to continue to play; however, patients with a low-risk stress
fracture may do so with activity modifications/relative rest.

Overview
Definition: a reversible compression within a closed fibro-osseous space that results in
decreased tissue perfusion and transient muscle ischemia
Most common in the lower leg of athletes who participate in running sports, particularly

Anterior compartment involvement is most common and comprises approximately 70% to

predictable surgical outcomes.

most commonly runners, and are younger than 30 years. Despite predominantly

Overview
Spondylolysis is an isolated defect in the posterior elements of the vertebrae, most commonly

May be unilateral or bilateral; single level or multilevel.
